cues.text: A Name Without a Story
Almost everything we would like to know about Clement is lost to us.
Ancient sources cannot agree on where he stands in the line of Peter's successors: some lists count him third, others fourth, after Linus and Anacletus .
Tertullian, writing around the year 199, records the tradition that Clement was ordained a bishop by St.
Peter himself, and St.
Jerome tells us that in his own day ‘most of the Latins’ believed the same.

Whatever the precise sequence, the ancient Church remembered Clement as standing close enough to the apostles to have their voices still ringing in his ears — a living bridge, however faint the record of him has become, between the world of the Twelve and the world that came after them.
A Letter to a Divided Church
The one thing about Clement beyond dispute is a letter.
Around the year 96, the church at Corinth fell into bitter faction: younger members had deposed presbyters who had served faithfully and without fault.

Word of the crisis reached Rome, and Clement, writing in the name of ‘the church of God which sojourns at Rome’ to ‘the church of God sojourning at Corinth,’ answered with a document of real pastoral authority — reasoning from Scripture and from Christ's own humility that ministers appointed by the apostles, and by their orderly successors, may not be removed at a faction's whim.
It is one of the oldest Christian writings outside the New Testament, and Corinth is known to have read it aloud in its assemblies for generations afterward.
Rome's First Word to a Sister Church
What strikes the careful reader is less any single argument than the letter's tone: a church far from Corinth writes as though it has every right to be heard, and Corinth, remarkably, listened.
Clement claims no title beyond the Roman church speaking through him, and the later sharp line between 'bishop' and 'presbyter' is not yet drawn cleanly in his pages.

Even so, here, in one of Christianity's earliest surviving documents outside Scripture, is Rome already speaking to a sister church with a confidence that the apostolic ministry it defends is not Corinth's alone to unmake — an early, often-noted witness to how quickly the Roman church came to feel responsible for the peace of the wider body of Christ.
A Legend of Exile and the Sea
Nothing certain survives about how or where Clement died.

The vivid story later ages told — exile to a Crimean quarry under Trajan, a miraculous spring struck from rock, and finally martyrdom by drowning with an anchor bound to his neck — is exactly that: a later story.

The Catholic Encyclopedia states plainly that the account cannot be traced earlier than the fourth century, and the two writers closest to Clement's own era, Eusebius and Jerome, say nothing at all of any martyrdom.
What can be said is that by the sixth century the tradition was well established, and that in the ninth century Sts.
Cyril and Methodius carried relics believed to be Clement's own to Rome, where they rest beneath the ancient basilica of San Clemente that still bears his name.
Legacy
We know Clement chiefly by one act of pastoral courage: a letter written not to advance himself but to hold a suffering church together in charity and right order.

Every pastor who has ever had to write a hard letter to a community not his own, trusting truth spoken in love to be received, finds in Clement an unlikely companion — a man history remembers less for who he was than for what he was willing to say.

The Church keeps his feast on November 23 and honors him, through the anchor of his legend, as a patron of mariners: fitting enough for a shepherd whose one sure legacy is a single letter that, after nineteen centuries, still holds.
